title: The Window · 14
paragraphs: (Of course Nancy had gone with them, because Minta Doyle had asked her to, with that mute look of hers, holding out her hand just as Nancy was escaping after lunch to her attic, away from the horror of family life. Then she supposed she had to go. She didn’t want to. She didn’t want to be dragged into it all. For all along the road to the cliff Minta kept taking her hand. Then she would drop it. Then she would take it again. What did she want? Nancy asked herself. People did want something, of course; because when Minta took her hand and held it, Nancy, against her will, saw the whole world spread out below her, like Constantinople seen through a mist, and then, however heavy your eyes, you had to ask, “Is that Santa Sofia?” “Is that the Golden Horn?” So when Minta took her hand, Nancy asked, “What is it she wants? Is it that?” And what was that? Here and there (as Nancy gazed down at life spread out below) something rose out of the mist—a pinnacle, a dome; prominent things with no names. But whenever Minta let go of her hand, as she did when they raced down the hillside, all of it—the dome, the pinnacle, whatever had been poking up through the mist—sank back into it and was gone.

Minta, Andrew noticed, walked rather well. Her clothes were more sensible than most women’s. She wore very short skirts and black knickerbockers. She’d jump right into a stream and flounder across. He liked how reckless she was, but he could see it wouldn’t do—one of these days she’d kill herself in some idiotic way. Nothing seemed to frighten her—except bulls. The mere sight of a bull in a field and up went her arms and off she ran, screaming, which was of course just what would enrage a bull. But she didn’t mind confessing it in the slightest; you had to give her that. She was a dreadful coward about bulls, she said, she knew. She thought she must have been tossed in her baby carriage when she was tiny. She didn’t seem to care what she said or did. Now all of a sudden she flung herself down at the edge of the cliff and started singing some song about
Damn your eyes, damn your eyes.
Everyone had to join in the chorus and shout it out together:
Damn your eyes, damn your eyes.
but letting the tide come in and cover all the good hunting grounds before they reached the beach would be a disaster.

“A disaster,” agreed Paul, leaping to his feet; and as they slid and scrambled down, he kept quoting the guidebook about “these islands being justly celebrated for their park-like prospects and the extent and variety of their marine curiosities.” But it wasn’t quite right, Andrew felt, picking his way down the cliff—all this shouting and damning your eyes, this slapping him on the back and calling him “old fellow” and the rest of it; it wasn’t quite right. That was the trouble with taking women on walks. On the beach they split up. Andrew went out onto the Pope’s Nose, took off his shoes, rolled his socks up inside them, and left that couple to look after themselves; Nancy waded out to rocks of her own and searched pools of her own and left that couple to look after themselves. Crouching low, she touched the smooth, rubbery sea anemones that clung like lumps of jelly to the side of the rock. Brooding, she made the pool into the sea, and the minnows into sharks and whales; she held her hand up against the sun and threw vast clouds over this tiny world, bringing darkness and desolation, like God himself, to millions of ignorant, innocent creatures; then all at once she pulled her hand away and let the sunlight pour down. Across the pale crisscrossed sand stalked some fantastic leviathan, high-stepping, fringed, gauntleted (she was still making the pool bigger), and slid into the vast cracks of the mountainside. And then, as her eyes slid imperceptibly up above the pool and came to rest on the wavering line where sea met sky, on the tree trunks that steamer smoke set wavering on the horizon, all that power sweeping savagely in and inevitably pulling back held her hypnotized. And the two sensations, of that hugeness and of this tininess (the pool had shrunk again), flowering inside it, made her feel tied hand and foot, unable to move, under the intensity of feelings that shrank her own body, her own life, and the lives of everyone in the world, forever, to nothing. So she brooded, crouched over the pool, listening to the waves.

Then Andrew shouted that the sea was coming in, so she went leaping and splashing through the shallows to the shore and ran up the beach, and her own impulsiveness and her wish to move fast carried her right around behind a rock, and there—oh heavens!—were Paul and Minta, in each other’s arms! Kissing, probably. She was outraged, indignant. In dead silence she and Andrew put their shoes and stockings on, and neither said a word about it. They were actually rather snappish with each other. She could have called him when she saw the crayfish, or whatever it was, Andrew grumbled. Still, both of them felt, it isn’t our fault. They hadn’t wanted this horrid nuisance to happen. All the same, Andrew was irritated that Nancy should be a woman, and Nancy that Andrew should be a man; and they tied their laces very neatly and pulled the bows rather tight.

Only when they had climbed all the way back to the top of the cliff did Minta cry out that she had lost her grandmother’s brooch—her grandmother’s brooch, the one ornament she owned—a weeping willow (they must remember it) set in pearls. Surely they’d seen it, she said, tears running down her cheeks: the brooch her grandmother had pinned her cap with until the last day of her life. And now it was lost. She would rather have lost anything else! She was going back to look for it. They all went back. They poked about and peered and searched. They kept their heads down low and spoke in short, gruff bursts. Paul Rayley hunted like a madman all around the rock where they’d been sitting. All this fuss over a brooch really wasn’t right at all, Andrew thought, while Paul told him to make a “thorough search between this point and that.” The tide was rising fast. In a minute the sea would be over the spot where they’d sat. There wasn’t a ghost of a chance they’d find it now. “We’ll be cut off!” Minta shrieked, suddenly terrified. As if there were the least danger of that! It was the bulls all over again—she couldn’t control her feelings, Andrew thought. Women couldn’t. Poor Paul had to calm her. The men (Andrew and Paul at once turned manly and unlike their usual selves) held a brief council and decided to stick Rayley’s cane in the ground where they’d been sitting and return at low tide. For now, nothing more could be done. If the brooch was there, it would still be there in the morning, they promised her; yet Minta went on sobbing all the way to the top of the cliff. It was her grandmother’s brooch; she’d rather have lost anything but that. And yet Nancy felt that, though she might really mind losing her brooch, that wasn’t all she was crying for. She was crying about something else. We could all sit down and cry, Nancy felt. But what for, she didn’t know.

Paul and Minta went on ahead together, and he comforted her, telling her how famous he was for finding things. When he was a small boy he had once found a gold watch. He’d get up at daybreak, and he was certain he’d find the brooch. It seemed to him it would still be nearly dark, and he’d be alone on the beach, and somehow there would be a bit of danger in it. Still, he began assuring her he would definitely find it, and she said she wouldn’t hear of him getting up at dawn: it was gone: she knew it was: she’d had a feeling when she put it on that afternoon. And privately he made up his mind not to tell her, but to slip out of the house at dawn while everyone slept; and if he couldn’t find it he’d go to Edinburgh and buy her another, exactly like it but lovelier. He’d show what he could do. And as they came out on the hill and saw the town’s lights below, the lights springing out one by one seemed like the things that were going to happen to him—his marriage, his children, his house. And once more, as they came out onto the main road, shaded by tall bushes, he thought of how they would withdraw into solitude together and walk on and on, he always leading, she pressed close at his side (as she was now). As they turned at the crossroads he thought what a terrifying ordeal he had been through, and that he had to tell someone—Mrs. Ramsay, naturally, for it took his breath away to think what he had been and what he had done. Asking Minta to marry him had been far and away the worst moment of his life. He’d go straight to Mrs. Ramsay, because somehow he felt she was the one who had made him do it. She’d made him think he could do anything. No one else took him seriously. But she made him believe he could do whatever he liked. All day today he had felt her eyes on him, following him everywhere (though she never said a word), as if she were saying, “Yes, you can do it. I believe in you. I expect it of you.” She had made him feel all that, and the moment they were back (he searched for the lights of the house above the bay) he would go to her and say, “I’ve done it, Mrs. Ramsay; thanks to you.” And so, turning into the lane that led to the house, he could see lights moving about in the upstairs windows. So they must be terribly late. People were dressing for dinner. The whole house was lit, and after the dark, the lights made his eyes feel full, and walking up the drive he said to himself, childishly, Lights, lights, lights, and said it over again in a daze, Lights, lights, lights, as they came into the house, staring around him, his face quite stiff. But good heavens, he told himself, reaching for his tie, I mustn’t make a fool of myself.)
